sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse Metacritic score is only behind 5 of the series' most beloved entries
sources.text: It also ranks slightly lower than Evil Empire's own Dead Cells: Return to Castlevania DLC Castlevania: Belmont's Curse reviews are in, and its Metacritic score is one of the highest in the Konami series' 40-year history, even if it doesn't quite hit the praise garnered by the most beloved games in the franchise. After a hiatus that has lasted just over a decade, Castlevania is getting its first brand new game in years this week, with Castlevania: Belmont's Curse having a lot riding on it for a lot of fans. Thankfully, it looks like things have gone down well, as the Castlevania: Belmont's Curse Metacritic score is sitting at 86 after 45 critic reviews, which as far as the series at large goes, is one of the strongest scores to date. In fact, the only Castlevania games with a higher score are some of the most beloved games in the series. Namely the GBA trilogy of Circle of the Moon (91), Harmony of Dissonance (87), and Aria of Sorrow (91), as well as Aria's sequel, Dawn of Sorrow (89), and, of course, Symphony of the Night – namely its Xbox 360 port at 89 and the PS1 original at 93. It also ranks lower than Vampire Survivors' Ode to Castlevania DLC (95) and Dead Cells' Return to Castlevania expansion (88) – which was developed by Belmont's Curse developer Evil Empire. In the GamesRadar+ Castlevania: Belmont's Curse review , social media editor Serena Cherry awards the game four out of five stars, saying, "Beautiful and challenging, Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse offers a rich, gothic world of puzzles to solve and enemies to whip. With a stunning blend of fast-paced traversal action and compelling storytelling, this game proudly honours the Belmont legacy in exciting new ways." Currently the majority of the game's reviews are dubbed "Positive" by Metacritic, with multiple outlets giving the game full marks. Elsewhere only eight reviews gave a "Mixed" score, with the game picking up a number of three out of five or seven out of 10 ratings. Castlevania: Belmont's Curse was born out of "a sense of urgency," producer says, and if we have to wait 10 years for the next game, "the whole thing is meaningless." He has also written for the likes of PC Gamer, Eurogamer, VG247, Play, TechRadar, and others. He's typically rambling about Metal Gear Solid, God Hand, or any other PS2-era titles that rarely (if ever) get sequels. sources.name: Polygon
sources.title: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse Reviews Hail a Triumphant Return
sources.text: If you haven't noticed, Konami is back, and the once-great Japanese publisher is finding its feet again by farming its properties out to hungry young developers all over the world. This has worked pretty well for Silent Hill, and now it's Castlevania's turn with Castlevania: Belmont's Curse. The first mainline installment in the vampire action series in more than 10 years, Belmont's Curse was made by Dead Cells support studio Evil Empire. (The groundwork for this collaboration was laid with the 2023 mashup Dead Cells: Return to Castlevania .) It looks like Konami's strategy has worked again. Castlevania: Belmont's Curse has strong reviews, the majority hailing it as a triumphant return for, and smart modernization of, the series. But some critics query whether it has really captured the Castlevania spirit. Currently, the game's average rating on the review aggregation sites sits at 86 on Metacritic and 85 on OpenCritic . Leading the cheering squad is GameSpot's Steve Watts , who called Belmont's Curse "one of the best Castlevania games, and one of the best metroidvania games, of all time" in a 10/10 review. Watts hailed the "sprawling map bursting with mysteries to uncover, joyous traversal tools that make roaming the map feel great, a story that balances a macabre tone with occasional lightness, a cast of creative and well-drawn characters, and hands-down the best combat of any Castlevania game — in fact, among the best combat of any 2D action game, period." Like many other reviewers, IGN's Scott White liked the new hero, Rose Belmont, and was impressed by the sharp and responsive combat, but felt that the latter came at the expense of some of Castlevania's classic characteristics, including the RPG system, and its unique feel. "So much else of what usually sets this series apart within this genre has been smoothed over with Belmont’s Curse , which leaves the whole package feeling a bit like a really solid metroidvania wearing a superficial Castlevania skin," White wrote. "There isn’t even a dagger to throw, which just feels kind of wrong. [Rose] doesn’t even start the game with a whip." This wasn't a problem for Game Informer's Charles Harte , who noted that Belmont's Curse , while technically a sequel to Castlevania 3 , follows on from the first two seasons of Netflix's Castlevania anime. "Arguably, it's a better sequel to the show than the game; the art style and character designs have clear anime inspirations, and many voice actors, including Trevor Belmont, reprise their roles," Harte said in a glowing 9.25/10 review. Harte also loved the new tarot card system, which unlocks upgradeable spells and also inspires some of the biggest treasure-hunts in the game. Like IGN's White, The Guardian's Harper Jay MacIntyre noted a shift toward "twitch-based action" in Belmont's Curse and said it "may annoy purists, but you can't call it dull." MacIntyre's three-star review criticizes the focus on Super Meat Boy-style platforming gauntlets over puzzle-solving, and some uneven pacing. "This may be the most virtually striking Castlevania since 2002’s Harmony of Dissonance and sometimes it’s also the most inventive and brain-teasing," MacIntyre wrote. "In other moments, you’ll be bored to bloody tears." But taken on its own merits, Belmont's Curse is "a near-perfect Metroidvania," according to Polygon's own Elijah Gonzalez . "By combining throwback appeal with razor-sharp gameplay built on the brilliant Dead Cells , Evil Empire’s latest lives up to Castlevania’s legendary status. From its bold use of color that makes the gothic visuals pop, to a new card-based Arcana system, Belmont’s Curse breathes new life into these games while honing in on what makes this series special." Castlevania: Belmont's Curse will be released on Oct. 15 for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X. A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction Release Date Confirmed
sources.text: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction has a release date: February 4, 2027. Bitmap Bureau, the developer behind Terminator 2D: No Fate, worked with Mattel and the retro team at Clear River Games on the old-school brawler, which launches digitally and physically on Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S. Two physical versions of the game will be available via Limited Run Games. The standard physical release costs $29.99, and the Collector’s Edition costs $99.99. Dragon Pearl of Destruction is inspired by the much-loved ‘80s animated series, and you can see that come through in pixel-art and 2D gameplay. The playable characters are He-Man, She-Ra, Man-At-Arms, and Teela, and you can play solo or co-op (two-player local co-op). There are 13 stages, including the Royal Palace, the Vine Jungle, and Snake Mountain, and famous villains such as Skeletor, Evil-Lyn, Beast Man, and Trap Jaw. You’ll also bump into the dark sorceress Shokoti and the Shadow Beasts. The Collector’s Edition includes lunchbox style packaging, pin badges, a mini-power sword, and an acrylic standee featuring He-Man riding Battle Cat, among other things. The contents of both physical editions are detailed below. We previewed He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction in August and thought it could be the first ever good He-Man game. It comes following the release of Amazon’s Masters of the Universe, which struggled at the box office but found success on Prime Video. Wesley is IGN's Managing Editor. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe Dragon Pearl of Destruction's lunchbox is a perfect '80s throwback
sources.text: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe Dragon Pearl of Destruction is a Bitmap Bureau-developed (in collaboration with Mattel) game that brings the iconic 80s cartoon to life as a Streets of Rage-style brawler. With its collector's edition being handled by Limited Run Games, there was no denying that the game would be bundled with a feast of physical merch, but I wasn't expecting a throwback quite like a lunchbox. The $99.99 (via Limited Run Games) Collector's Edition, no matter if it's the Switch, PS5, or Xbox version, includes the plastic lunchbox, which feels just as equivalently '80s as the original series. Growing up, I often received my cousin's lunchboxes as hand-me-downs, and a metal He-Man lunchbox was a staple of their childhood, and later mine. All it's missing is a matching Thermos flask and the faint smell of old fruit and salt and shake crisps to be one of the most truly nostalgic collector edition releases. Pre-orders for the He-Man and the Masters of the Universe Dragon Pearl of Destruction Collector's Edition are available now through November 22, 11:59 PM ET. If you want more unique collector's editions based on iconic Mattel toys, Barbie Rewind pre-orders are available for £59.99 at Amazon, and the Deluxe Edition includes a full-sized Barbie doll. Saturday Mornings in my '90s childhood were often spent having to use my cousin's hand-me-downs, and He-Man (and She-Ra) were a big part of that. Often it was the toys and old videotapes that made their way into my possession, but lunchboxes were also commonplace, which is why I'm pretty privy to this Limited Run Games release. Often the brand's fancy collector's editions include statues of varying quality, and this one is not exempt. There is a 4.9-inch Mini Power Sword and an acrylic standee showing He-Man riding Battle Cat included, but the lunchbox feels the most authentic. In fact, despite it not being included as a numbered release, this lunchbox puts this version up there as one of the better editions I've seen from the retailer. I'd much sooner have it in my collection than the falling-apart statuette included with my Limited Run Games ClockTower Rewind release. It's nice to see that despite all the physical tat that's bundled within its $99.99 MSRP, which also includes a pin set and a mini comic book, there's a physical copy of the game too. If you pre-order this collector's edition, you also get a physical copy of the game on the platform of your choice, and an alternative steel case to keep it in. Rockstar should maybe be taking notes if they choose to give the GTA 6 Collector's Edition another shot. If you are thinking of grabbing this collector's edition, I recommend pre-ordering sooner rather than later. While the pre-order window remains open until November 22, these Limited Run Games releases can be perfect fodder for eBay resellers. Love securing games as soon as possible? Check out our GTA 6 pre-order and Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time pre-order pages. Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+. Ever since I first held a NES controller in my hand I've been obsessed with gaming, and the hardware it runs on. I could hook up a NES and SNES to a telly, without instructions, before I could walk. Even now, nothing is more exciting then taking a console, or handheld, out the box for the first time and setting it up. This obsession transformed into a love of games and game music, which lead to my music degree and dream of becoming the Scottish Nobuo Uematsu. After sharing my love of games through music, I began to share my love through words on sites like TechRadar and iMore. This lead to becoming a Hardware staff writer for PCGamesN, and later the Senior Tech Writer for Dexerto, covering all things Steam Deck, PlayStation and Nintendo. With that experience, I was able to level up as Hardware Editor for GamesRadar+, where I'm still just as Nintendo, PlayStation and gaming tech obsessed as ever. sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: The God of War Laufey Collector's Edition is the latest to release without the game itself
sources.text: No game, but you will get an expensive light-up statue starring everyone's favorite gelatinous cube God of War Laufey is getting a pricey collector's edition with some fancy goodies – but it's bad news if you actually wanted to play the game itself. The year is 2026, and you expected to get a copy of a game included with the expensive special edition you're buying? Preposterous! But no, seriously, this trend of collector's editions being sold without the games they're for – not even including a download code – is a baffling one, and after GTA 6 did the same thing earlier this month, Sony is continuing it with its upcoming God of War title. Not exactly a great look with everyone still annoyed about its plans to kill physical discs . Revealed by PlayStation today, the £129.99 (PS Direct UK, we're still waiting on US pre-orders to drop ) God of War Laufey collector's edition, or rather the "Collector Box" as Sony is calling it (perhaps to better reflect the lack of actual game), includes just three items – a mini artbook and a 51-card "Oracle Deck" being two of them. The star of the show, and undoubtedly the thing that puts the cost of the box as high as it is, is a light-up statue of Faye. The store page doesn't say how large this statue is, but it's made of resin, and shows Faye attacking some foes while her trusty cube companion Phranque smiles on in the background. At least, I assume he would be if he had a face. Strangely, the Collector Box hasn't yet been listed in the US at the time of writing, but in the UK, it'll cost you £130. Without the game included in that price, that essentially means fans are going to be paying a minimum of £200 for their full God of War Laufey experience next February. At least God of War: Laufey is actually getting a physical disc release, even if you won't be getting it in a fancy box with a statue. Sony has announced that it's killing physical releases for new PlayStation games starting in 2028 – a decision that's gone down horribly and is continuing to see backlash months later. And fans aren't happy with Sony for leaving the game out of Laufey's Collector Box, either. The God of War Ragnarok Collector's Edition also didn't come with a physical disc, but it did at least include a download code, which was something. This time, not so much. Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more "I remember when collector's editions used to come with games. Not liking this new trend," one responds on Twitter. "Doesn't even come with a sad little code," says another . Well, one saving grace is that it's significantly cheaper than GTA 6's own Collector's Box, anyway. Similarly not including a game code, Rockstar's box of merch costs £350 / $400 , but hey, at least you get an ugly gator statue with it, and that's obviously what fans have been waiting the last 13 years for. The Last of Us director apologizes for using God of War Laufey as an example of "lack" of innovation in AAA: "This isn't the team's fault." I'm GamesRadar+'s Deputy News Editor, working alongside the rest of the news team to deliver cool gaming stories that we love. After spending more hours than I can count filling The University of Sheffield's student newspaper with Pokemon and indie game content, and picking up a degree in Journalism Studies, I started my career at GAMINGbible where I worked as a journalist for over a year and a half. I then became TechRadar Gaming's news writer, where I sourced stories and wrote about all sorts of intriguing topics. In my spare time, you're sure to find me on my Nintendo Switch or PS5 playing through story-driven RPGs like Xenoblade Chronicles and Persona 5 Royal, nuzlocking old Pokemon games, or going for a Victory Royale in Fortnite. sources.title: God Of War Laufey Collector’s Edition Doesn’t Include The Game, This Time On Purpose
sources.text: God of War Laufey no disc no sale PS5 Sony I refuse to allow this to become normal. No matter how many times it happens, it’s completely deranged, and we should keep calling it out.Â God of War Laufey ‘s so-called Collector Box has been revealed (thanks PushSquare ), containing a light-up statue, a 51-card deck and an art book, and…no copy of the game. Looking likely to cost around $130 (the U.S. version is yet to be announced, but the UK’s version is Â£130 ), you’ll still have to spend another $70 on top if you want to play the game the box is allegedly about. First popping up on the Spanish PlayStation Store, the Caja de Coleccionista de God of War Laufey seemed to have leaked early, before other nations starting revealing the same, with the U.S. still to go. The box contains a resin statue of Faye fighting enemies with her long, pointy sword, complete with purple ribbon, accompanied by lit blue cubes for maximum garishness. There’s also a deck of Oracle cards, 51 in total, each with a unique illustration based on Faye’s journey, and apparently capable of Everywhen magic. And last of all there’s the requisite “mini artbook,” because for over $100 you cannot expect a full-size one. And that’s it. That’s a very expensive statuette, deck of cards, and pamphlet, and only more ridiculous when you consider you haven’t actually bought a copy of the game in the process. Of course,Â God of War Laufey ‘s deal looks positively sensible when compared to Rockstar’s reveal of a $400Â GTA 6 collector’s edition that also doesn’t come with the game. But the practice remains absolutely ludicrous given it’s the difference of putting a piece of paper with a code printed onto it. Given the items in the box can’t cost much more to produce than about $60 at a push, it’s pretty grim that it’s not in there by default, even putting aside the inherent weirdness of it. And unlikeÂ GTA 6 ,Â Laufey is getting a physical release. Making this even more strange is the debacle that occurred during the lastÂ God of War ‘s release. 2023’sÂ Ragnarok had two different (far better) special editions, the Collector’s and the JÃ¶tnar Edition, both of which were supposed to come with a download code for the full game andâinexplicablyâ a steelbook display case that didn’t contain a disc . This then got worse when people discovered the download code hadn’t been included . This was at least an error that Sony worked to resolve, but three years later the absence is now entirely deliberate. As for why this ever happens, one possible reason is cost-saving. If you are selling the game on multiple consoles, you need to produce multiple versions of the collector’s edition, and that means different SKUs, different box designs, and so on. Except, Laufey is a PS5 exclusive, so this doesn’t apply at all. It simply seems to be an exercise in finding out what can be gotten away with while still making money. At least the box doesn’t contain a disc case to not put a disc in this time, I guess. Donât miss the latest reviews, news and tips. Sign up for our free newsletter. sources.name: Polygon
sources.title: God of War Laufey’s Collector Edition Continues a Frustrating Trend
sources.text: Sony is taking a page out of Rockstar’s book After Sony Spain accidentally posted the collector’s box for God of War Laufey early, the company revealed the U.S. edition of the bundle . Going for $149.99, the box includes three collector’s items: a Faye statue, a 51-card Oracle deck, and a mini artbook. Despite the hefty price, there’s a notable exclusion: this collector’s edition doesn’t include a disc or digital download code for the game . " God of War Laufey game sold separately," the fine print at the bottom reads. While it seems a bit baffling that a collector’s edition for a video game wouldn’t include said video game, Sony isn’t the first company to pull this trick. Rockstar recently announced a $399.99 collector’s box for Grand Theft Auto 6 that similarly doesn’t include the game, instead being stuffed with merch based on a fictional show from the thing we haven’t played yet. It includes sunglasses, hats, shot glasses, and other paraphernalia, which frankly doesn’t seem to justify nearly $400. In defense of Laufey ’s collector's edition, resin statues can be pretty pricey, coming in at the $50 to $200 range for ones that seem to be similar in size to the "Light-Up Faye Statue” (although it’s difficult to say for sure, since the product page doesn’t give an exact measurement for some reason). In the Oracle deck, "Stunning bespoke illustrations adorn each card with meaning inspired by Faye’s journey." As for the Mini Artbook, the product description promises "incredible concept art that shaped the world of God of War Laufey." The bundle releases on Feb. 16, 2027, alongside the game. Between Grand Theft Auto 6 and God of War Laufey , these “collector’s boxes” seem tied to a recent uptick in fandom-driven collector culture , as prices for trading cards and other nerd-culture staples on secondary markets boom. One notable overlap is that Rockstar and Sony have come under fire for ditching support for physical games. “Physical” copies of Grand Theft Auto 6 won’t include discs , and will instead come with a download code in a case. Laufey will have a physical release with a disc, but Sony recently announced its controversial decision to stop producing physical copies of its games starting in 2028 . These collector’s boxes feel like a preview of an all-digital future where instead of these collector’s editions being centered around a physical game case and disc, they are there to sell you (probably overpriced) trinkets. It’s a bit bleak.

sources.title: Sifu será lançado para Android e iOS em outubro; veja trailer do port
sources.text: Sifu , jogo de artes marciais da Sloclap, será lançado para Android e iOS. A desenvolvedora anunciou a versão mobile do game, com estreia prevista para 12 de outubro deste ano. “A mesma ação, a mesma aura, a mesma atmosfera. Agora, na palma da sua mão”, anunciou a Sloclap no X. Na mesma publicação, a empresa anexou um trailer de gameplay da nova versão. A jogatina de Sifu no mobile parece ser idêntica à versão para PC e consoles, com os mesmos cenários, personagens e chefões – portanto, tudo indica que seja um port. No vídeo, são exibidos os botões virtuais adaptados para a tela touchscreen, que permitirão experimentar a porradaria mesmo sem um controle dedicado . Sifu é um jogo de artes marciais com combate rápido, em que o jogador acompanha o protagonista em uma jornada de vingança. O combate é cheio de combos interessantes e marcado pelo forte foco em parries e desvios. Porém, o que deixou Sifu mais relevante é o sistema de vidas. Durante as fases, cada morte do personagem principal não é necessariamente fatal, mas faz com que ele envelheça alguns anos – o que o deixa mais forte com o tempo, mas também mais frágil. O game over acontece quando o protagonista fica velho demais para retornar após uma derrota. Reconhecido jogo de artes marciais da Sloclap, Sifu foi lançado para PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5 e PC em fevereiro de 2022; chegou ao Nintendo Switch meses depois e, em 2023, foi lançado para Xbox One e Xbox Series X | S. O jogo já está listado na App Store e na Play Store. No iOS, vai custar US$ 7,99 (R$ 39,80, em conversão direta) ; no Android, o preço ainda não aparece na loja, mas já é possível fazer o pré-registro, que notifica o usuário quando o jogo estiver pronto para download. O jogo conquistou uma boa nota na análise do Voxl anos atrás . Ao longo do tempo, muito conteúdo foi adicionado ao game, incluindo novas arenas, cosméticos desbloqueáveis e mais desafios que estendem as horas de conteúdo. Quer ficar por dentro das novidades do mundo dos games? sources.text: “Death row inmates reality show x death game adventure” game BUZZ or DIE will launch PC via Steam on October 28, publisher Kodansha and developer Bon announced . It will support English, Japanese, and Simplified Chinese language options. A demo is available now. Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page : BUZZ or DIE is a point-and-click game where death row inmates enter a death-match game show. You and a man named Sagishima will be participating together. The rules are simple. Dive into your opponent’s mindscape and search for secrets. Turn those secrets into content and make a short video. Gain the most Likes from the audience to win. The winner receives a pardon and the chance to have one wish granted. The loser receives not only death…but an eternity of humiliation as a slave android model. Witness the passions and fury of the world’s worst criminals in this gripping video-game drama. We hope you enjoy.

stories.title: Haunted Chocolatier 'More of an Action RPG' Compared to Stardew Valley, ConcernedApe Says
stories.summary: Eric Barone, aka ConcernedApe, has discussed the difference between his all-conquering indie game Stardew Valley and his hotly anticipated follow-up, Haunted Chocolatier.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: Haunted Chocolatier 'More of an Action RPG' Compared to Stardew Valley, ConcernedApe Says
sources.text: Eric Barone, aka ConcernedApe, has briefly discussed the difference between his all-conquering indie game Stardew Valley and his hotly anticipated follow-up, Haunted Chocolatier . Barone announced Haunted Chocolatier back in 2021, but amid ongoing work on his phenomenally successful Stardew Valley, progress on the follow-up has been slow going. Indeed, in June, Barone admitted to feeling somewhat embarrassed to have to keep on saying he was still working away on the game. “Feels kinda dumb posting this same thing over and over, but that’s the reality,” he said at the time. In a new interview with GQ (thanks, Eurogamer ), Barone touched on what to expect from Haunted Chocolatier when it eventually comes out, and it sounds more different from Stardew Valley than I had expected. It’s set in a more “metaphysical” locale, for a start, and in terms of gameplay it’s more of an action RPG. “It is still what I call a town game,” Barone said, “But it’s more of an action RPG — the main focus is more about adventuring, finding equipment and getting more powerful. There are monsters, there are boss fights. It's for the people in Stardew Valley that go into the mines. That's what I do, honestly.” In June, Barone admitted fussing over every last detail in a bid to make Haunted Chocolatier as close to perfect as humanly possible . “I am being very thoughtful about every aspect of the game,” he said at the time. “The things in the game which the player will be interacting with or using very often need to be ‘perfect.’ They need to be seamless, clear, intuitive, satisfying, aesthetic.” He used the example of iterating on the recipe book for making chocolates, which sounded like a significant challenge. “To me, it’s not a simple task, as I torture myself over every last detail,” he said. “This is a UI you will be using fairly often, so it has to be perfect. You need to be able to accomplish your goal with the minimal number of clicks. There needs to be just the right amount of data presented to the player: not so much as to be overwhelming, but not so little as to be trivial or mundane. And the way that this data is laid out on the page is crucial… If the data is all clustered together, it will be disgusting to look at. The data needs to be grouped into compelling, intuitive and easy to read/understand groupings. It needs to look appealing and intriguing. And this is just the bare minimum, that players will likely take for granted. If all of that is accomplished then the player is now comfortable while perusing the recipe book. But I want more than just comfort. I want to delight the player. All of this typically requires me to iterate on something several times before I’m satisfied with it.” Barone also explained why he didn't want to show Haunted Chocolatier off too much at this stage of development. “Partly, it feels like I’m serving a half-baked bread. I would rather serve a fully baked bread,” he said. “Also, I know that many parts of the game will likely evolve and change before release, so if I reveal them early, I risk disappointing players if the final product does not match their expectation. Fortunately, I’m in a position where I don’t need to market the game, so I can take my preferred approach.” Haunted Chocolatier is so far without a release date, as is Stardew Valley 1.7 update, which Barone isn’t working on directly. Earlier this year, he explained his current way of working in an interview with IGN . “Well, part of the reason why I've expanded my team a little bit is so that hopefully I can spend more time working on Haunted Chocolatier," he told us in February. "And it's worked out pretty well so far, I would say. On 1.7, the approach we're taking is that I am like, you might say the creative director and I'm involved with like, 'Okay, here's what we're going to do. Here's some of the ideas.' Then I let the team work on that. And then meanwhile, I'm working on Haunted Chocolatier. "At some point in 1.7's cycle, I will get heavily involved, because I feel like my hand needs to touch every part of the game, every aspect of the update. I need to go over it and adjust it or at least approve everything. So it will require a lot of my time anyway, but I think the balance has been a little bit more shifted, so that I can spend more time focused on Haunted Chocolatier. And I think it's been working out pretty good. That's been a big change from the 1.3 update or 1.1 or something where it's completely me. I had no time to work on a new game. So that has changed. "It is difficult because it's hard to shift gears, I guess. If I'm thinking about Haunted Chocolatier, it's difficult to be like, 'Okay, I'm going to one day of the week or two days of the week work on Stardew Valley.' That's not how my brain works. I'm all in one thing or the other. So I've been trying to work on that. I feel like it requires a lot of discipline, which I'm always working to improve on." We interviewed ConcernedApe and chatted about topics such as the addition of two new marriage candidates with 1.7 , the one secret players still haven't found yet , and why there isn't a Stardew Valley TV show yet . We also chatted with the Stardew Valley community about what the game has meant to them over the years. Wesley is IGN's Managing Editor. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

sources.name: Eurogamer
sources.title: Stardew Valley creator's new game, Haunted Chocolatier, is "more of an action RPG" than farming sim
sources.text: "It's for the people that go into the mines." Stardew Valley creator Eric Barone, has given a new interview - and finally revealed a little more information about his upcoming title, Haunted Chocolatier. In a wide-ranging interview with GQ , which tackles topics ranging from creative burnout to the importance of 'cosy gaming', Barone also slips in some new information about what we can expect from his highly-anticipated Stardew Valley follow-up. And it's all rather surprising. Per the interview, this game is a much more action-oriented affair than the cosy homesteading of Stardew Valley: "It is still what I call a town game," he told GQ, "but it's more of an action RPG - the main focus is more about adventuring, finding equipment and getting more powerful. There are monsters, there are boss fights." For anyone that's played Stardew Valley, this won't be a massive shock; there is a combat element to the game, though mostly it's sequestered to one portion of the map - the mines that hold some of the game's rarest materials. If you had fun venturing in there at night to fight slimes and horde minerals, you're going to like Haunted Chocolatier, it seems. "[The new game] is for the people in Stardew Valley that go into the mines. That's what I do, honestly," said Barone. Elsewhere, Barone noted that Haunted Chocolatier is a more "metaphysical" experience than Stardew Valley - which makes sense, I suppose, given its connection to the world of ghosts and spirits - and that "no one's playing the game until I'm ready to show it". Hence, there's still no word on a solid release date. The last update we had on the game was all the way back in January, where Barone noted "I'm alive, the game is still in development" , following up previous statements he made alluding to the fact that the world of Haunted Chocolatier is bigger than Stardew Valley. As for when it's coming out? "The bottom line is, I don’t want to give a release date," Barone said at the start of the year. "The game will come out when it's done." If you want to learn more about the man behind one of video gaming's biggest phenomena of the past few generations, I'd urge you to read the full GQ piece: it's a sensitive, comprehensive look at a man that boasts many talents, yet is also humble and grounded. If you're interested in the musical side of his development process, I profiled Barone once in my column at The Guardian.

stories.title: Game Developer veteran Chris Kerr launches Vertical Slice, a games publication "giving workers a voice and holding power to account"
stories.summary: Chris Kerr, former Senior Editor of GDC sibling Game Developer (formerly Gamasutra) has launched a new subscription-funded publication to deliver "incisive, bold reporting for video game industry professionals" that "scrutinises with intensity and integrity without having to worry about conflicting commercial interests." Read more

sources.name: GamesIndustry.biz
sources.title: Game Developer veteran Chris Kerr launches Vertical Slice, a games publication "giving workers a voice and holding power to account"
sources.text: The outlet, which is entirely funded by reader subscriptions, will also include a free repository of pitch and design documents Chris Kerr, former Senior Editor of GDC sibling Game Developer (formerly Gamasutra) has launched a new subscription-funded publication to deliver "incisive, bold reporting for video game industry professionals" that "scrutinises with intensity and integrity without having to worry about conflicting commercial interests." Vertical Slice , which launched today and will be free to read until November 2nd, is aimed at "developers who care deeply about the art form and wellbeing of their peers," Kerr tells GamesIndustry.biz, along with "executives and industry leaders who value uncompromising honesty over pandering puff pieces." Subscription pricing starts at £7.45 per month. Kerr left Game Developer along with several other contributors and its EIC, Danielle Rindeau, in September, with Rindeau saying that reporting honestly is " not something one can do without editorial independence ". Vertical Slice will carry news and features alongside an archive of pitch and design documents called the The Repository, intended to serve as a resource for other developers. After the paywall launches in November free users will be able to access files in the Repository section and "select articles", says Kerr, but the majority of the site's output will require a subscription to read. "We want to become known for providing developers with the knowledge required to hone their craft and change the video game industry for the better," he says. "That could mean spotlighting a new funding initiative, amplifying the voice of unionising workers, asking experts to contextualise a trending news story, producing long-form investigative journalism to surface a pressing issue, or simply chatting with devs about their rad new thing." "It will always mean giving workers a voice and holding power to account by cutting through the noise to find the truth." Kerr has self-funded the site, which will rely on reader subscriptions for the bulk of its revenue. His initial goal is 500 monthly subscribers or 650 annual, which would match his previous salary, but once he has covered that and his operating costs he wants to "funnel every last penny back into the publication," he says. "I'm not starting Vertical Slice to amass untold riches. I simply want to do the work I value in service of an audience in need of top-quality reporting." The site will not carry advertising, save for sponsorship of its database of design and pitch documents which "will be made possible through contributions and sponsorships from like-minded partners who believe in the need for greater transparency within the video game industry." "I want to create a clear divide between that and our journalistic output," he says. "I'm working with a third-party sales agency to ensure Vertical Slice reporters (including myself) will never be directly involved in those conversations." Kerr is the sole staff member at launch, but plans to "immediately reinvest in editorial as soon as I achieve sustainability," and has already commissioned multiple freelance contributions from ex-Polygon reporter Nicole Carpenter. He says the "most affirming aspect of going independent" has been chatting with other independent outlets including Aftermath, People Make Games, Game File and Manchester-based startup The Mill . "The media industry has reached a critical juncture," says Kerr. "It's to dispel the notion that journalism is a low-grade commodity to be consumed freely. Meanwhile, journalists need to become comfortable asking people to pay for their craft." "Meaningful journalism demands hours upon hours of invisible labour before you can even think about putting pen to paper. Late night source calls. Tracking down and then poring over dense documentation. Fact-checking every last sentence. Even as someone who's been doing this for over a decade, I regularly feel I should be grateful to simply be doing the job — and I truly am — but that doesn't negate the fact that work is work."

sources.name: Kotaku
sources.title: Former Editor Of Game Developer Launches Vertical Slice, A ‘Fearless’ New Trade Publication
sources.text: As more and more long-established games publications shrink, vanish, or consolidate, an ongoing rise in independent journalism is working hard to keep the fire lit. Today, weâve got a brand new publication on the block; a trade publication, to be precise. Itâs called Vertical Slice , and itâs run by long-time investigative games reporter Chris Kerr. Kerrâs been reporting about games for 15 years, on the trade beat for about 13, and at Game Developer for around 11, concluding as its senior news editor. He left the publication at the end of last month, trading the (relative) stability of a full-time role for the great unknown of owning his own website. As someone currently enjoying the former type of stability, I had to knowâ¦why? âI feel like I can do my best work outside the confines of a publication that is owned by a globally traded corporation with wildly different commercial interests,â Kerr said. âOften those interests can overlap. That’s not always the case. I suspect that is true of many publications that have a corporate backer. And, you know, there are many positives to being corporate-owned, right? It offers you more security. I had a pension. That was greatâ¦But I feel like in order to produce journalism that is as punchy as it can be, properly fearless. You need to potentially go it alone, depending on your circumstances.â Eschewing that stability then, how is this possible? Kerr is funding this with his own savings, saying heâs been âquite sensibleâ with his money over the last decade. Heâs also, at the start, going it alone, so he only has to pay his own salary. But itâs still a risky venture. âIt is scary,â he says. âI believe in it. I don’t know what else I want to do.â Kerr describes Vertical Slice as âfearless reporting that inspires, informs and interrogates.â The key there is reporting: Vertical Slice is a news-focused publication. No guides, no reviews. Itâs not an aggregation platform, though there will be a newsletter readers can subscribe to for a summary of whatâs on the website. And specifically, he wants to be breaking news stories every day. I note that thatâs ambitious, but Kerr just says heâd âpick up where I left offâ at Game Developer .Â Kerr is deeply passionate about the state of games media, and what he hopes will be his own forthcoming role in it with Vertical Slice. âI want to build something that’s mine,â he says. âI want to build something that hopefully stands the test of time, that people can rally behind, that does give workers a platform to speak out against, you know, misconduct, injustice, all of those thingsâ¦I want to give those people a voice because ultimately they’re the ones who are making the video games that we all play.â And also quite critically, most of the website will be paywalled, no ads. There will be some free articles each week, and the site will also launch with a library of design documents and pitch decks submitted by developers such as OuterSloth and Kitfox Games, which will also be free. When we spoke, Kerr was still working out the exact pricing, but he compares his vision of it to be like paying for a newspaper from a local newsstand every day. âI think readers need to just start picking a lane,â he says. âAnd it’s like, look at all the AI aggregation. We’re all being subjected to death by a thousand cuts because AI is going for our jobs, people are getting laid off. People don’t want to pay for reporting, you know what I mean? Like, we’ve got to figure out how to make this work. And I think there is a fairly simple equation, which is just, if you enjoy a journalist’s work, pay for it. Like, it sounds simple and it maybe sounds a bit reductive, but it sort of is simple, isn’t it, really?â Kerrâs ambitious. He talks about wanting to eventually hire on more full-time writers, mentor up-and-coming journalists, take freelance columns, eventually get developer-written articles on the websiteâ¦his dream is to someday have a fully-functioning newsroom of between five and ten people, though he admits thatâs years down the road, and dependent on a lot of success between now and then. âI want to create pathways for new talent,â he tells me. I point out that while many other excellent independent publications have emerged in recent years, none have quite managed to do what heâs proposing yet, certainly not at the scale he wants. Whatâs Kerr doing differently that makes him think Vertical Slice will break through? âI suppose why I believe I can make this work is I don’t see anyone else doing it,â he says. âI mean, particularly in the trade space, right. I know for a fact that millions of people have read my articles over the past few years. And it’s just a fraction of those people were willing to pay. Not everyone, just like a super small percentage. I’d be able to break even and probably bring someone else on. And as soon as you’ve broken even, I want to reinvest from that point just into the site, whether that’s bringing on a regular freelancer with a view to them potentially as a full-time hire, whether it’s starting up a podcast, something.â Kerr good-naturedly tells me that heâs aware of the ways in which this venture could fail, but heâs made his peace with it. If Vertical Slice doesnât work out, he says heâll âmelt away into the sunset and maybe become a soccer journalist.â But for now, he feels what matters most is that he at least tries to build something for both his future, and the future of the space. âI think we’re all grateful to be doing what we’re doing, but is it actually working for us in terms of the career prospects? In terms of our ambitions as, you know, healthy, functioning adults with our own personal lives who want to go on holidays, maybe want to have kids, whatever it is? Like, how could you do that, in an industry that won’t give you any sort of runway? That’s what I want to offer. And again, I know it

stories.title: A New '3 for 2' Board Game Sale Is Now Live at Amazon and Target

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: A New '3 for 2' Board Game Sale Is Now Live at Amazon and Target
sources.text: If you’ve been eager to build up your tabletop collection for some fall game nights, you’re in luck: Target and Amazon are both running hefty ‘3 for 2’ sales on board games, puzzles, and toys. I took some time to compare selections between the two sales, and Target actually comes out on top in terms of just how many options are includedin the deal. However, if you’re looking for a specific game, you may find a better individual discount at Amazon. The massive retailer just had its October Prime Day sale last week, and some discounts haven’t gone away just yet. Both sales work in the same way: Add three eligible items to your cart, and the cheapest of the three will be automatically discounted to $0 at checkout. I’d recommend some strategy around the price of the three items you include to maximize that “cheapest item” discount. The deal also stacks, so you’ll get one free game or puzzle for every three you add to your cart. Both sales include a mix of both traditional tabletop and more quick-playing card games. If you don’t already have something in mind, I’d think about whether your collection is missing something quick and casual or a longer campaign for a more dedicated group. If you’re just trying to build up a solid collection, you’ll never regret picking up classics like Catan . There’s also a splattering of themed editions. These include, of course, ridiculous amounts of Monopoly variants, though you also have entirely new franchise releases like the Fourth Wing board game . As someone who gets way too much satisfaction out of knowing the Pokedex, I’d personally recommend the Pokemon edition of Guess Who . Why do I think Target takes the win on this one? Well, besides including classics like Clue that Amazon skipped out on, Target is also including tons of expansions. So instead of getting three separate games, you could get Cards Against Humanity plus two of its expansions. Or you could just invest in a bunch of expansions for games you already own. Both sales also include tons of jigsaw puzzles from major companies like Ravensburger, RoseArt, and theory11. Sure, these might not offer the same level of competition as a board game, but they still offer an opportunity for some social collaboration. Blythe (she/her) is an Audience Development Coordinator at IGN who spends way too much time in character customization screens and tracking down collectibles.

sources.title: Satisfactory: The Board Game Preview
sources.text: Automation and factory-building games have become pretty popular over the past few years, with Coffee Stain Studios' Satisfactory being one of the stars of the genre. I have always admired the sprawling conveyor belts and mega structures of the factory-building powerhouse from a comfortable distance, dipping my toe into the waters with messy (but kind of functional) factories of my own. Soon, factory builders will have a whole new way to build out their process, as Mood Publishing, the same publisher behind Hitman: The Board Game , is looking to bring the beloved factory sim to your tabletop with Satisfactory: The Board Game and the launch of their latest crowdfunding campaign over on Gamefound . We were sent an early prototype copy to check out, in addition to playing a demo with the game’s designer, David Thor Fjalarsson, to see if a tabletop game can capture and refine the Satisfactory experience down to the size of a kitchen table-sized factory. In Satisfactory: The Board Game (referred to simply as "Satisfactory" going forward), designed by David Thor Fjalarsson, up to four players will have to mine, refine, and upgrade their factories in an effort to earn the most FICSIT points before the space elevator is finished. The turns themselves are surprisingly straightforward; on your turn, you will perform two actions, either build something, move around the map, or have your factory do its work. Once each player has taken their turn, the production phase occurs, where everyone's mines will activate, drilling for one of the three basic materials—limestone, iron, or copper—and existing materials will move down their conveyors towards getting refined into better resources. Then, the whole cycle repeats itself. Even in my first game, by the time my group had reached the second or third round, we had the flow down. The game itself takes place on a large hex-grid representation of the video game's massive world, with random creatures and biomes that get placed during setup, along with various material-rich points where mines can be placed. The “Move” action is pretty self-explanatory, allowing you to move your piece up to a number of spaces equal to your movement value, with some spaces that can only be crossed once certain technologies or vehicles have been built. Landing on a point can grant you resources, or allow you to claim one of the tokens mentioned earlier. If you prefer to get some extra work in at your factories, you can instead opt for the “Workshop” action, which lets you either move a beltline of resources down a spot or refine a single block of material into a higher-tier version, which is a crucial component for when you build. Speaking of building things, the “Build” action was my favorite, and what I would consider the core thing to do in this game. At any time, players will have access to build their staple devices—extractors, refineries, et cetera—in addition to a random pool of cards of varying tiers that get unlocked over the course of the game. These cards, like the Jet Pack to help you get around quicker or weapons to tackle the wildlife, are a great help, but the main structures you can construct have an added little treat to them. Depending on what you build, you will have a bonus action that you can take, determined by what you have built. Building a miner, for instance, will allow you to immediately build a Belt, which will then trigger the Belt’s bonus, giving you a free movement action, or the Constructor, giving you an extra action you can take on your turn. Stringing together these bonuses to create some wild turns was some of the most fun I had playing Satisfactory. When it comes to playing, Satisfactory's tabletop adaptation has opted for a competitive “race for points” experience for its main game, instead of the cooperative focus from the PC title — though the promised final game will include a co-op and solo modes as well. That said, don't expect to be bombing or taking out the other players' extractors and belts with some cardboard corporate terrorism within the game. Instead, once a player has claimed a tile by building something on it, no other player can develop on it, though they can still cross over with no issue. Satisfactory can still be “mean,” but it’s more like cleverly getting in the way or making expansion for your opponents annoying as opposed to turning the planet into a battlefield. This sort of headbutting really only comes out when you start getting to the three- or four-player counts. At two players, because both players have so much more space, I was surprised and impressed with how different Satisfactory manages to feel. During my two-player game, with far less worry about my factory getting locked in by other players, I instead was able to focus and work out how best I wanted to try and optimize (as optimized as you could get in a game like this after only a couple plays) my system. It honestly felt like I was playing different games based on the player counts, with two players focusing on optimizing and planning out turns to maximize earning points, while with three, and especially four, figuring out how best to expand my factory and balancing blocking resources from the others was much more in the forefront of my mind. Oddly enough, I think I actually enjoyed the puzzley nature of the lower player count more, as both of us weren’t forced into conflict with one another, and I could better test out what Satisfactory offers. In one two-player game, I focused on maxing out my basic resource production, getting all of my extractors online as fast as I could, and expanding my reach to a few farther-out “rich” tiles, which further let me produce more of the resource during production phases. Having an almost overabundance of these cheaper resources allowed me to quickly gobble up and complete the early-game Milestones, netting me a bunch of points and rocketing me out into the lead, faster than the elevator could take me. sources.title: Star Wars Galactic Racer's devs tested its roguelite progression system by turning it into a board game
sources.text: "You can't know if you can feel the system until you can play the system." Years ago, I read that Jake Solomon prototyped the Firaxis reboot of XCOM by making a simple board game version. Something rudimentary that could be played in the office on scrap paper to get ideas across and figure out where the fun would be, without having to commit. But it's surprising to hear the same idea being used for a game as different from XCOM's turn-based tactics as Star Wars Galactic Racer. As Fuse Games' creative director Kieran Crimmins told Eurogamer , "You can't know if you can feel the system until you can play the system." And so the early prototype of this high-speed arcade racing game was indeed a board game. "You know, modern engines are so capable that you can do a lot of it in-software," CEO Matt Webster said, "but there's still something [about that which is] not as fast as getting a written idea down. From a board game perspective, you sort of decouple yourself from a particular prototype and you're talking about moment-to-moment." Specifically, the board game simulated Galactic Racer's progression system. Its rewards differ based on the event, but typically offer tuning points to spend on one of three random stats, and maybe a part for your speeder that will affect its abilities or grant a bonus related to a specific status effect. After several races you get to go shopping, and spend the credits you've earned on more upgrades and parts, or a whole new ability. It's a progression system right out of a roguelite, with new unlocks added to a pool so they might appear in future runs, and each run handing out tuning points that can be used for permanent upgrades that carry over between them. Not something you expect in a racing game, and a system that presumably needed a bit of road testing to find the fun. "There's a prototyping tool for every kind of system that you want to prototype," Crimmins said, "and the one that you pick should be the one that gets you there the quickest, and gets you to validate the emotion the quickest. So when it came to upgrades and meta progression, I can do a board game in a day. I mean, I say 'board game'. A lot of it is Post-its and a scribble and some dice. But we're trying to validate those feelings as quickly as possible. So you just pick the best tool for the moment." 2026 games : All the upcoming games Best PC games : Our all-time favorites Free PC games : Freebie fest Best FPS games : Finest gunplay Best RPGs : Grand adventures Best co-op games : Better together Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team. sources.name: GamesIndustry.biz
sources.title: Dragon Quest creator Yuji Horii releases game he says he made with AI in about 30 minutes
sources.text: Horii said AI means people can now make a decent game alone, even if they can't draw or program Yuji Horii, the creator of Dragon Quest, says he has produced a new game using AI in about 30 minutes. Horii shared the game, a text-based police interrogation game, in a post on X/Twitter . He said it took about 30 minutes to make, and told players "don't press the boost button." He said that with AI, people can now make a decent game alone by giving it instructions, even if they can't draw or program. He compared this to making The Portopia Serial Murder Case in 1983: "I came up with the story myself, drew the pictures myself, did the programming myself, and created the game all by myself." In the game, players question a 72-year-old suspect, a former locksmith named Komiya, over a break-in at a pawnshop's safe. Players have until a lawyer arrives at 11pm to draw out statements, then confront the suspect's lies with evidence. The higher his agitation, the easier he is to crack, but if his resistance reaches 100, he stays silent. Horii has previously worked with AI in games, and Square Enix partnered with Google earlier this year to add a Gemini-powered chatbot called Chatty Slimey to Dragon Quest X. In a Famitsu interview , also earlier this year, Horii defended the decision, saying that the chatbot makes it easier for people to start interacting with AI. He is also involved with Dragon Quest 12 and Next: The Portopia Serial Murder Case , which was announced in September for 2027. Unity recently unveiled Unity Spark , a browser-based tool for building 3D games with text prompts, which will launch in beta later this year on Google's Playground.

sources.title: Dragon Quest Creator Has a New Game, but It's AI-Generated
sources.text: Yuji Horii, creator of the Dragon Quest franchise, used Claude to develop and release a browser-based video game in less than an hour. While it resulted in some backlash, Horii expressed how impressed he was with the tool and praised AI for significantly reducing development time and increasing efficiency. Square Enix has been particularly open about increasing its AI usage to improve company efficiency. It wants to hand over the majority of quality assurance and troubleshooting tasks to AI . It has also used AI technology in an attempt to improve text-based adventure games, such as The Portopia Serial Murder Case , a Yuji Horii game originally published in 1983. Horii himself has no issues praising AI for how helpful it can be for game development. Recently, he used Anthropic's Claude AI tool to generate a text-based browser game. He compares the development process to Portopia 's 40 years ago, when, to create a game, he had to come up with a story, draw art, and program the code; it could take months or even years to release a game, but now, he was able to create and release his new browser game within 30 minutes simply by giving AI a prompt. In Horii's newest game, players find themselves in an interrogation room. By asking questions and providing evidence, they must catch the subject in his lies and corner him before time runs out or he shuts down. It's a fairly short game that crime enthusiasts would otherwise enjoy, but it could easily have been made by humans. AI has become a major topic of concern in the gaming world. It has led to hundreds of layoffs as companies push to use it to increase efficiency. Big companies like EA have strongly encouraged AI use to boost productivity while saving money . Most recently, Epic Games has told employees to stop hand-writing code and use artificial intelligence instead. According to Epic Games' CEO Tim Sweeney, developers have been asked to "retool for maximum AI acceleration" so they can produce "more and better stuff." This comes after the announcement that a Star Wars and Marvel crossover game developed by Epic has been delayed. Dragon Quest is a popular franchise with many hardcore fans who fell in love with the early games in the series due to the creativity and imagination displayed in their fantasy worlds. It was the hard work of human creators, like Horii himself or Akira Toriyama, who was in charge of character design, that breathed life into these worlds. One has to wonder if fans will show the same level of appreciation for games that are entirely developed by AI.
